reason: Both pages are accurate against facts.md: 14/72 for the cheap model, 58 vs 72 GPT calls, break-even prices of 0.11 cents and 13.3 cents, and costs at 5 cents that match the cost scenarios ($50.00 / $40.50 / $66.18 per 1,000). A is a compact 7-step card. Each step adds one idea: the dot grid, test-002 through both checks, the 14/58 sort, the cost breakdown, and an animated price sweep that shows the lines crossing. At 390 px its step 6 slider, the verdict line, the bars and the crossing chart all fit on one screen, so moving the price shows the answer flip at once. A also gives the Wilson range (12% to 30%) and a clear rule in step 7. B is richer for a finance reader: monthly dollars, an invoices-per-month input, preset break-even buttons and a tappable grid of 72 invoices. But on a phone the saving chart sits about 1,000 px below the slider, its labels are about 8 px, and the tap tooltip covers the step buttons. That makes B harder to use as the price explorer the request asked for.

A: Step 6 slider readout and verdict disagree after a drag (slider says 14.1 cents, verdict says 'At 14.0 cents a call').
Chart labels and the step 7 'Before you rely on it' notes are small at phone width, and the legend pairs 'Cheap model (Qwen)' blue with the repeat-check line, which is confusing.

Prices are given in fractions of a cent (0.11 cents, 0.05 cents) on a log axis, which finance managers will find less natural than dollars per month. Loss assumptions for wrong payments are not mentioned.
B: The saving chart's text is about 8 px at 390 px width and hard to read.
The slider and its outcome chart are far apart on a phone (one long scroll between them), so the price-to-winner link is hard to see while dragging.
Tapping a grid square opens a tooltip over the step 1-5, Back and Next controls. No uncertainty range is given for the 14/72 rate.
